title: Is Day Porter Service Included in Standard Cleaning or an Extra Charge? A Contract Audit Guide
seoTitle: Extra Charge Day Porter Services: Included vs Add-On Contract Audit
metaDescription: Extra charge day porter services can add $1,500–$11,000+ monthly. Learn what base retainers include vs work-order billing, then audit quotes side by side.
excerpt: Standard nightly janitorial contracts almost never include a day porter, yet many quotes blur the line with vague phrases like daytime support. This audit guide shows US office managers exactly which porter tasks belong in a retainer, which get billed as work orders, and how to catch hidden extra charges.
quickAnswer: Day porter service is almost never included in a standard nightly cleaning contract; it is either added to the monthly retainer as a dedicated line (about $1,516–$2,815 for 2 hours per weekday up to $6,062–$11,258 for a full-time porter at $35–$65 per hour) or billed as separate work orders with $90–$135 per-visit minimums. Audit the scope for named hours, task lists, response times, and consumables so daytime support is not quietly billed as extras.

blocks.text: The Short Answer: Porters Are Almost Always a Separate Line

A standard US office cleaning contract is built around after-hours production work: vacuuming, trash and recycling removal, restroom cleaning and restocking, breakroom sanitation, dusting, and hard-floor care, priced at roughly $0.05–$0.20 per sq ft per visit depending on size and frequency. That scope assumes the building is empty. Day porter service—someone on-site during business hours—requires a separate labor commitment, and reputable vendors price it as its own line item. When a proposal claims daytime support is included at no added cost, it usually means one of three things: a short courtesy check by the night supervisor, on-call response billed per incident, or porter labor quietly folded into an inflated base rate.

None of those is necessarily wrong, but each has a different cost profile. Your job during the contract audit is to identify which model you are actually buying, and to make sure the language matches the invoices you will receive.
Retainer vs. Work Order: How Porter Tasks Are Typically Billed

blocks.caption: Where common daytime tasks land in US janitorial contracts
rows: Restroom checks and restocking during the day
$15 – $30 per restroom per visit if ad hoc
$15 – $35 per visit for full partition cleaning
Conference room setup and furniture moves
Hourly at $35 – $65, more for heavy moves
Weekend or holiday rates at about 1.5x
Project quote or $0.03 – $0.06 per sq ft per month amortized program

blocks.title: Red flag: daytime support with no hours listed
blocks.text: If a proposal mentions daytime support, porter availability, or on-site presence without stating hours per day, days per week, and named tasks, assume you will be billed per call. Ask the vendor to convert it into either a fixed retainer line or a published work-order rate card before signing.
How to Audit a Contract for Hidden Porter Charges

items.name: Find the porter line and its unit
items.text: Locate whether porter labor is priced hourly, as a monthly lump sum, or per square foot. Convert everything to hours using $35–$65 per hour as the national benchmark.

items.name: Check the hours math
items.text: Confirm monthly hours equal daily hours x days per week x 4.33. A 4-hour, 5-day porter should show about 86.6 hours, not 80.

items.name: Match tasks to frequencies
items.text: Every porter duty should have a frequency or trigger. Vague duties become extra charges.

items.name: Read the exclusions page
items.text: Scope exclusions such as furniture moves, event setup, biohazard cleanup, and exterior glass reveal what will be billed separately.

items.name: Locate the work-order rate card
items.text: Require published rates for call-ins, after-hours, weekends, and holidays, plus minimum hours per dispatch.

items.name: Review three months of invoices
items.text: For existing contracts, compare billed extras against the porter scope. Repeated extras for the same task mean the retainer is under-scoped.

blocks.text: When Folding the Porter Into the Retainer Saves Money

If your office generates daytime requests most days, a retainer is cheaper. Consider a 20,000 sq ft office averaging twelve call-ins per month for restroom restocks, spills, and conference resets. At a $135 minimum each, that is $1,620 per month for reactive service with no guaranteed response time. A scheduled 2-hour weekday porter costs $1,516–$2,815 per month and covers those issues proactively, plus lobby glass and breakroom resets. Above about ten call-ins monthly, the retainer usually wins on both cost and appearance.

Conversely, an office with two or three daytime issues a month should stay on a work-order model. Paying for 43 hours of porter time to solve three spills is waste. In that case, negotiate lower call-in minimums or a bank of prepaid hours at the retainer rate.
Equipment and Supplies: Another Hidden Add-On Zone

Porter quotes also differ on who supplies tools and consumables. Some vendors include basic equipment in the hourly rate; others itemize it. Make sure the porter has the right gear for the duties you are paying for. Daily conference-room glass touchups go faster with an 18-inch anodized aluminum squeegee and microfiber washer kit on an 8-foot telescopic pole, such as the Unger Professional kit. Spill response requires fold-flat 25-inch multilingual wet-floor A-frames—the Rubbermaid Commercial 6-pack covers multiple restroom cores—to meet slip-and-fall prevention practices. For cubicle tops, blinds, and monitor stands, disposable electrostatic high-reach dusters like the Swiffer Heavy Duty 360 with 3-foot extension and no-scratch fibers keep daytime dusting quiet.

items: Consumables supplied by the vendor typically add $0.012–$0.025 per sq ft per visit; confirm whether porter restocking uses your paper or theirs.
Equipment rental lines for auto-scrubbers or carts should be disclosed, not buried in the hourly rate.
Green Seal or Safer Choice chemical requirements should apply to porter and night crews equally.
Wet-floor signage and PPE are vendor responsibilities under OSHA general duty and HazCom expectations.

blocks.title: Compliance terms to write into the porter scope
blocks.text: Require a certificate of insurance listing your company and landlord as additional insureds, OSHA HazCom training with SDS sheets on-site, and bloodborne pathogens training under 29 CFR 1910.1030 for porters who handle restroom or bodily-fluid cleanup. Specify that biohazard incidents beyond small spills are excluded and escalated to a certified remediation vendor.

faqs.q: Why don't nightly cleaning contracts include a day porter?
faqs.a: Nightly contracts are priced on production rates around 3,500 sq ft per hour in an empty building. A day porter is paid for presence during occupied hours, which is a different labor model. Including it would raise the per-sq-ft base rate significantly, so vendors list it separately to keep bids comparable.

faqs.q: How much extra does a day porter add to a monthly cleaning bill?
faqs.a: At $35–$65 per hour and 4.33 weeks per month, a 2-hour weekday porter adds about $1,516–$2,815 per month, a 4-hour porter about $3,031–$5,629, and a full-time porter about $6,062–$11,258. Ad hoc work orders carry $90–$135 per-visit minimums plus premiums for same-day, weekend, or holiday calls.

faqs.q: What should a porter work-order rate card include?
faqs.a: It should list the hourly rate, minimum hours per dispatch, same-day and after-hours premiums, weekend and holiday multipliers, consumables pricing, and response-time commitments. Without a rate card, every extra becomes a negotiation after the fact.

faqs.q: Can I convert recurring extra charges into a porter retainer mid-contract?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Most janitorial agreements allow scope changes by written amendment. Bring three months of invoices showing recurring work orders and ask the vendor to price a fixed porter shift. If call-ins exceed about ten per month, the retainer is typically cheaper.

faqs.q: Are porter duties covered by the vendor's insurance?
faqs.a: They should be, but confirm the COI covers daytime operations in occupied space and that general liability limits meet your lease requirements, often $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate. Slip-and-fall risk is higher during occupied hours, so wet-floor signage and documented training matter.
